nodes.label: Distance, Midpoint, and Directed Segment Division
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in the 2D Cartesian coordinate plane, the Pythagorean theorem, similar right triangles, and solving linear equations. Derives the Euclidean distance formula d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) by constructing the horizontal-vertical right triangle between P₁(x₁, y₁) and P₂(x₂, y₂), establishes the midpoint formula M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2), and derives the section formula P = ((n x₁ + m x₂)/(m + n), (n y₁ + m y₂)/(m + n)) for the point dividing segment P₁P₂ internally in ratio m : n via similar right triangles (highlighting the common order trap of pairing m with P₁ instead of P₂). Trains using coordinate distances and midpoints to classify triangles (scalene, isosceles, equilateral, right via Pythagorean converse) and quadrilaterals, test collinearity, recover an unknown endpoint from a midpoint or ratio point, and translate simple equidistant locus descriptions (such as points equidistant from two fixed points) into algebraic equations. Stays strictly in 2D planar coordinates and leaves line equations, point-to-line distance, circles, and formal coordinate proofs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Equations of Lines, Slope, and Parallel/Perpendicular Conditions
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in linear equations, similar right triangles, basic angle geometry, and tangent of angles in [0, π) from Trigonometric Functions (used solely for inclination). Establishes slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) as a point-independent invariant via similar right triangles, connects it to angle of inclination α ∈ [0, π) via m = tan α (undefined at α = π/2 for vertical lines), and builds fluency moving among point-slope y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), slope-intercept y = mx + b, intercept x/a + y/b = 1, and general linear form Ax + By + C = 0—emphasizing that general form unifies oblique, horizontal, and vertical lines (x = c) without missing vertical cases. Proves the parallel criterion (m₁ = m₂ or both vertical) and the perpendicular criterion (m₁ m₂ = −1, or one horizontal and one vertical) using congruent/similar slope triangles. Applies line equations and 2×2 linear systems to find line intersections, perpendicular bisectors, altitudes, and medians of coordinate triangles (computing circumcenter, orthocenter, and centroid). Leaves point-to-line distance, coordinate theorem proving, and 3D lines/planes to subsequent or separate modules.

nodes.label: Point-to-Line Distance and Equidistant Line Loci
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes planar distance and linear equations to derive and apply the formula for the perpendicular distance from a point P₀(x₀, y₀) to a line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C| / √(A² + B²). Proves the formula cleanly in 2D without 3D vectors—either by computing the foot of the perpendicular through P₀ (slope B/A) and simplifying the distance, or via similar right triangles formed by a vertical/horizontal segment from P₀ to the line—carefully checking horizontal (A = 0) and vertical (B = 0) cases as well as the sign interpretation of Ax₀ + By₀ + C (opposite signs on opposite sides of the line). Applies the formula to compute the distance between parallel lines |C₂ − C₁|/√(A² + B²) (stressing the necessary condition that both lines must first be scaled to identical A and B coefficients), compute triangle altitudes and areas in coordinates, and derive equations of the two perpendicular angle bisectors of intersecting lines as the locus of points equidistant from both lines. Enables the learner to compute exact point-to-line and line-to-line distances and set up line-distance locus conditions, directly supporting circle tangency in a later lesson.

nodes.label: Coordinate Proofs of Planar Geometric Theorems
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes distance, midpoint, section formulas, and parallel/perpendicular line criteria to prove general planar Euclidean theorems algebraically. Develops the essential strategic placement bridge: positioning a general figure on the coordinate axes (e.g., placing one vertex at the origin and one side along the positive x-axis, and using convenient symbolic coordinates like (2a, 0) and (2b, 2c) to avoid fractions) without specializing the figure (explicitly guarding against the misconception of assigning numeric coordinates or accidentally assuming a general triangle is right or isosceles, or a parallelogram is a rectangle). Works through classic coordinate proofs—the triangle midsegment theorem, bisection of parallelogram diagonals, perpendicularity of rhombus diagonals, concurrency of triangle medians at ((x₁+x₂+x₃)/3, (y₁+y₂+y₃)/3), and Thales' theorem for a right angle inscribed in a semicircle—verifying every geometric claim through exact algebraic identities on slopes, midpoints, and distances. Enables the learner to set up lossless general coordinates and write complete coordinate proofs of planar theorems.

nodes.label: Circles: Standard Form, Completing the Square, and General Form
nodes.explanation: Builds on the planar distance formula and assumes completing the square from Quadratic Equations and Functions to develop the analytic geometry of circles. Derives the standard equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² (r > 0) directly as the locus of points at constant distance r from center (h, k), and interprets interior (< r²) and exterior (> r²) regions. Expands standard form into general circle form Ax² + Ay² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (A ≠ 0) and reverses the process by dividing by A and completing the square in both x and y, explicitly classifying the three algebraic outcomes: a real circle (r² > 0), a degenerate single point (r² = 0), and an empty locus (r² < 0). Trains constructing circle equations from geometric givens—center and radius, endpoints of a diameter, center and a point on the circle, or three non-collinear points (via substituting into x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 to solve a linear system, or intersecting perpendicular bisectors). Enables the learner to convert fluently between standard and general circle forms, identify degeneracies, and write circle equations from geometric data. Leaves line-circle tangency and non-circular conics to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Line-Circle Intersections, Chords, and Tangent Lines
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes circle equations and point-to-line distance (together with quadratic discriminants from entry background and perpendicularity of lines from earlier ancestors) to analyze interactions between lines and circles in the plane. Develops two equivalent classification criteria for a line L and a circle of center C and radius r: the algebraic discriminant test (substituting L into the circle equation and checking Δ > 0 secant, Δ = 0 tangent, Δ < 0 disjoint) and the geometric distance test (comparing d(C, L) to r: d < r, d = r, d > r), showing when each method is cleaner. Trains computing chord lengths via the Pythagorean right-triangle bridge L_chord = 2√(r² − d²), finding the tangent line at a specified point P₀(x₀, y₀) on the circle using perpendicularity of the radius CP₀ (obtaining (x₀ − h)(x − h) + (y₀ − k)(y − k) = r²), and finding both tangent lines to a circle from an external point (setting d(C, L) = r for a line through the external point, carefully checking whether a vertical line is one of the tangents!). Also introduces intersection points of two circles by subtracting their general equations to obtain the linear common-chord/radical line. Enables the learner to solve tangency, chord, and intersection problems involving lines and circles.

nodes.label: Parabolas: Focus-Directrix Definition and Standard Equations
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the planar distance formula and horizontal/vertical lines (assuming completing the square and basic vertical parabola vertex form from Quadratic Equations and Functions) to redefine parabolas geometrically and analyze all axis-aligned orientations. Defines a parabola as the locus of points equidistant from a fixed focus F and a fixed directrix line L (not containing F), and derives the standard equations (x − h)² = 4p(y − k) (vertical axis) and (y − k)² = 4p(x − h) (horizontal axis) directly from d(P, F) = d(P, L). Interprets the signed focal parameter p (distance and direction from vertex to focus, opposite to directrix), axis of symmetry, focus, directrix, and latus rectum (focal chord of length |4p| providing two rapid graphing guide points). Trains converting general one-square equations Ax² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 or Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 into standard form by completing the square, recovering an equation from focus/directrix or vertex/point data, and solving applied reflector problems (e.g., finding the focal depth of a parabolic dish or bridge arch). Explicitly warns against confusing the coefficient 4p with p. Leaves ellipses, hyperbolas, and rotated parabolas to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Ellipses: Foci, Standard Equations, and Eccentricity
nodes.explanation: Builds on circles (specifically standard-to-general completing the square and the distance formula from its ancestor) to develop the geometry and algebra of axis-aligned ellipses. Defines an ellipse as the locus of points P satisfying PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a for two fixed foci F₁, F₂ separated by 2c < 2a, and carries out the double-squaring derivation of the centered standard equation x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with b² = a² − c² (explicitly contrasting c² = a² − b² with the Pythagorean hypotenuse formula so learners do not invert a and c). Extends to translated centers (h, k) for both horizontal major axis ((x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1) and vertical major axis ((x − h)²/b² + (y − k)²/a² = 1), identifying center, vertices, co-vertices, foci, major/minor axis lengths 2a and 2b (always with a > b > 0, spotting orientation by which denominator is larger), and eccentricity e = c/a ∈ [0, 1) (linking e = 0 to circles and e → 1⁻ to elongated ellipses). Trains converting Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (with A, C > 0) by completing the square—remembering to factor A and C before balancing the constant term and spotting point or empty degeneracies—and applies ellipse geometry to orbital aphelion/perihelion distances and semi-elliptical arches. Leaves hyperbolas and rotated ellipses to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Hyperbolas: Foci, Standard Equations, and Asymptotes
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes circles (completing the square in x and y, and the planar distance formula transitively) with linear equations and slopes to develop axis-aligned hyperbolas. Defines a hyperbola as the locus of points P satisfying |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a for two fixed foci separated by 2c > 2a, and derives the standard centered equations x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 (horizontal transverse axis) and y²/a² − x²/b² = 1 (vertical transverse axis) with c² = a² + b², explicitly contrasting orientation rules with ellipses: for a hyperbola, orientation is determined by which squared term is positive, and a may be smaller than, equal to, or larger than b. Extends to translated centers (h, k), derives the oblique asymptotes y − k = ±(b/a)(x − h) (or ±(a/b)(x − h)) by examining large-|x| behavior of y − k = ±(b/a)√((x − h)² − a²), constructs the central 2a × 2b guide rectangle to sketch branches accurately, and introduces eccentricity e = c/a > 1 (relating larger e to wider branches). Trains converting Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (with AC < 0) by completing the square—carefully handling the negative leading coefficient and spotting degenerate intersecting lines when the constant term becomes 0—and applies difference-of-distance modeling (such as acoustic or radio time-difference localization). Enables the learner to analyze, graph, and construct axis-aligned hyperbolas.

nodes.label: Translation of Axes and Classifying Axis-Aligned Conics
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas into a unified treatment of the general axis-aligned quadratic equation Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (with B = 0 and A, C not both zero). Formalizes translation of axes x = x' + h, y = y' + k as the geometric counterpart of completing the square—choosing (h, k) to annihilate both linear terms when AC ≠ 0 (centering the conic) or to shift the vertex to the new origin when AC = 0 (parabola). Establishes the rapid coefficient classification test (circle when A = C ≠ 0, ellipse when AC > 0 and A ≠ C, parabola when AC = 0 with one nonzero, hyperbola when AC < 0) alongside systematic algebraic verification of all degenerate cases (empty set, single point, single line, pair of parallel lines, pair of intersecting lines), emphasizing that inspection of A and C alone cannot distinguish a true conic from a degenerate one without completing the square or factoring. Also solves 2D nonlinear intersection systems (line-conic and conic-conic intersections via substitution or elimination, verifying geometric multiplicity up to four intersection points). Enables the learner to classify, translate to standard form, sketch, and intersect arbitrary axis-aligned conics, preparing directly for rotation of axes.

nodes.label: Rotation of Axes and Eliminating the xy-Term
nodes.explanation: Builds on axis-aligned conics and translation of axes, assuming Trigonometric Functions (unit-circle sine, cosine, and tangent for angles in (0, π) and right-triangle ratios) and explicitly deriving/supplying the local trigonometric bridges sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ, cos 2θ = cos² θ − sin² θ, and the acute half-angle formulas cos θ = √((1 + cos 2θ)/2) and sin θ = √((1 − cos 2θ)/2) for θ ∈ (0, π/2) so no separate identity course is silently assumed. Derives the planar rotation equations x = x' cos θ − y' sin θ and y = x' sin θ + y' cos θ (plus the inverse relations) geometrically by rotating the positive x- and y-axes counterclockwise through angle θ to unit directions (cos θ, sin θ) and (−sin θ, cos θ). Substitutes into Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 (B ≠ 0) to obtain the rotated coefficients and sets B' = B(cos² θ − sin² θ) + (C − A)(2 sin θ cos θ) = 0, deriving the elimination condition cot 2θ = (A − C)/B (with θ = π/4 whenever A = C, illustrated immediately on xy = k rotating to a standard hyperbola). Trains both special-angle rotations (θ = 30°, 45°, 60°) and non-special rational cot 2θ cases—constructing a signed reference triangle for 2θ ∈ (0, π) to get cos 2θ and then exact radical values of sin θ and cos θ via the acute half-angle formulas without calculator approximation—and sketching the resulting conic in the rotated x'y'-frame superimposed on the original xy-plane. Leaves rotation invariants and discriminant classification to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Rotation Invariants and Discriminant Classification of General Conics
nodes.explanation: Builds on rotation of axes to establish the algebraic invariants of the general 2D quadratic equation Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 and classify any planar conic without first carrying out a full rotation. Proves directly from the rotated coefficient formulas that the trace A + C and the quadratic discriminant Δ = B² − 4AC remain unchanged under any rotation of axes (A' + C' = A + C and B'² − 4A'C' = B² − 4AC), as well as under translations of axes. Uses the elimination rotation B' = 0 to deduce B² − 4AC = −4A'C', immediately establishing the complete discriminant test: B² − 4AC < 0 is elliptic (ellipse, circle when A = C and B = 0, point, or empty set), B² − 4AC = 0 is parabolic (parabola, parallel lines, coincident line, or empty set), and B² − 4AC > 0 is hyperbolic (hyperbola or pair of intersecting lines). Explicitly emphasizes the crucial caveat that Δ determines only the conic family, never ruling out degeneracies—training learners to combine rotation and subsequent translation (completing the square in x' and y', or directly factoring reducible quadratics like x² − xy − 2y² + x + y = 0) to separate nondegenerate conics from degenerate line/point loci. Enables the learner to classify general planar quadratics rapidly via invariants and carry out full rotation-plus-translation reduction to standard form.

nodes.label: Unified Focus-Directrix Characterization of Conic Sections
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on axis-aligned conics (and their eccentricities) to unify parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas under a single geometric definition. Introduces the focus-directrix ratio PF / d(P, L) = e for a fixed focus F, directrix line L not passing through F, and positive eccentricity e > 0, proving algebraically in Cartesian coordinates that e = 1 yields a parabola, 0 < e < 1 yields an ellipse with directrices x = ±a/e (or y = ±a/e) corresponding to foci (±ae, 0), and e > 1 yields a hyperbola with directrices x = ±a/e lying between the vertices and the origin. Shows how circles emerge as the limiting case e → 0 with directrices receding to infinity while a stays fixed. Enables the learner to compute directrices of ellipses and hyperbolas, write conic equations from focus-directrix-eccentricity data, and see the three non-circular conics as one continuous geometric family—staying strictly in 2D Cartesian coordinates without requiring polar coordinates.

nodes.label: Tangent Lines and Optical Reflective Properties of Conics
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing line-circle tangency (specifically discriminant-zero tangency) with axis-aligned conics to compute tangent lines and verify the optical reflective properties of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas purely algebraically without calculus. Applies the Δ = 0 intersection condition to derive the tangent line equation at a point (x₀, y₀) on a centered conic (obtaining the symmetric replacement pattern x² → x₀ x, y² → y₀ y, 2x → x + x₀, such as x₀ x / a² + y₀ y / b² = 1 for an ellipse, x₀ x / a² − y₀ y / b² = 1 for a hyperbola, and y₀ y = 2p(x + x₀) for y² = 4px). Uses these explicit tangent slopes and coordinate distances to verify the three classical focal reflection laws: rays parallel to a parabola's axis reflect through the focus, rays from one focus of an ellipse reflect to the other focus, and rays aimed toward one focus of a hyperbola reflect directly away from the other focus (linking to telescopes, whispering galleries, and Cassegrain reflectors). Enables the learner to find tangent lines to conics algebraically and justify their focal reflection properties.
